results.title: Sun: Facts - NASA Science
results.content:
Above the Sun’s surface are its thin chromosphere and the huge corona (crown). This is where we see features such as solar prominences, flares, and coronal mass ejections. The latter two are giant explosions of energy and particles that can reach Earth.

The Sun doesn’t have moons, but it’s orbited by eight planets, at least five dwarf planets, tens of thousands of asteroids, and perhaps three trillion comets and icy bodies. [...] The Sun rotates on its axis as it revolves around the galaxy. Its spin has a tilt of 7.25 degrees with respect to the plane of the planets’ orbits. Since the Sun is not solid, different parts rotate at different rates. At the equator, the Sun spins around once about every 25 Earth days, but at its poles, the Sun rotates once on its axis every 36 Earth days.

## Moons

As a star, the Sun doesn’t have any moons, but the planets and their moons orbit the Sun.

## Rings [...] The Sun could not harbor life as we know it because of its extreme temperatures and radiation. Yet life on Earth is only possible because of the Sun’s light and energy.

## Size and Distance

Our Sun is a medium-sized star with a radius of about 435,000 miles (700,000 kilometers). Many stars are much larger – but the Sun is far more massive than our home planet: it would take more than 330,000 Earths to match the mass of the Sun, and it would take 1.3 million Earths to fill the Sun's volume.

results.title: How Many Moons Does Each Planet Have? | NASA Space Place – NASA Science for Kids
results.content:
We on Earth have just one moon, but some planets have dozens of them. Others don’t have any. Which planets have moons, and which don’t?

Let’s go in order from the Sun.

  

## Mercury and Venus

Up first are Mercury and Venus. Neither of them has a moon.

Because Mercury is so close to the Sun and its gravity, it wouldn’t be able to hold on to its own moon. Any moon would most likely crash into Mercury or maybe go into orbit around the Sun and eventually get pulled into it. [...] Uranus has 29 known moons. Some of them are made partly of ice.

Lastly, Neptune has 16 known moons. One of Neptune's moons, Triton, is as big as dwarf planet Pluto.

  
 Neptune asks Uranus if theyhave enough moons. We've got a good number of moons, right?   
   

To learn more about the moons in our solar system, visit the NASA Solar System Exploration moons page.

article last updated July 31, 2026

### More about moons!

 a close up view of the asteroid Ida [...] Jupiter is the biggest planet and has the biggest moon, Ganymede. Cartoon illustration.   
   

## Saturn

As of June 2026, Saturn has 293 moons. And that’s not counting Saturn’s beautiful rings!

Saturn’s moons have great names like Mimas, Enceladus, and Tethys. One of these moons, named Titan, even has its own atmosphere, which is very unusual for a moon.

## How big is the Sun?

The Sun is the biggest object in our solar system, with a distance of 695,508 from to surface. It contains 99.86% of the mass of the entire solar system and could contain roughly 1.3 million Earths. [...] Sometimes the Moon comes between the Sun and Earth. If all three are aligned, the Moon can block the Sun entirely, casting a shadow on Earth and causing a solar eclipse. This is because even though the Sun is 400 times larger than the Moon, the Moon is 400 times closer to Earth. [...] ## Where is the Sun in the Milky Way?

There are an estimated 100 billion galaxies in the known universe. The Sun and its eight planets, including Earth, reside in one known as the Milky Way. Our galaxy is around one quintillion or 100,000 light years.
